owner: W1-17. The connective tissue: the answers whose nouns make the province's other 109 subjects askable.
why: build-graph.mjs reported 151 orphans — topics with authored text and no way in. 42 were advertised on an NPC's own `topics` array and are reachable in the running game; 109 were reachable by nothing at all. In Morrowind a subject becomes askable because somebody says the word in front of you, so these are answers, not an index.
house_rule: Every info carries both an actor and a cell, and this file sorts ahead of every file these topics are declared in, so the more-constrained info is authored above the less-constrained one under both Morrowind's first-match rule and infoFor()'s specificity score. No line here closes on a direction; check-prose measures that as `echo_direction` and ours already runs 2.82x the reference.

infos.x: Burning is what is done for a body the marsh will not take back. The marsh burial is the ordinary way, and the marsh does not take back a body it did not have a hand in. So a yard that burns as often as this one is saying something about how the dead here are being made. It is not said aloud at the yard.

Vaskh burns and Vaskh writes. Her book has a name, a weight and a tide in it for every one, and the book kept by the drowned court, the tally of the dead, has a number and nothing else. No clerk in this office has ever asked her to set the two down side by side. She finds that restful. I do not.

She won't take money for it, dry-one, and she won't take a name she hasn't been given, and when the water brings up a man no family claims she gives him one out of her own and writes it into the tally of the dead herself. There are eleven of her cousins in that book who never lived.
The smoke goes up behind the customs post most evenings and everyone in Soulrest knows what hour it is by it. Not one of us counts who goes on. Only she does.

Six feet of salt block and a gate no man of mine has opened. Stores, per the roll, and the old quarter behind it, per everybody else. Show me the requisition and I will walk you as far as the gate. I will not go past it.

It is not on the original survey, which is generally taken to mean it was built after, and the survey was not amended, which is generally taken to mean it was not built at all. In most accounts of Stormhold the wall simply appears, fully mortared, in a paragraph about drainage, with the old quarter already behind it.

My grandmother lived on the other side of it, in the old quarter, and came out. That's all she ever told anyone, and she told it in that order, and she said it like the second half was the strange part. Do you want the room facing it or not?
There's a family here still paying rent on a house behind it. The office takes the money. The office has said nothing about the house in nine years.

It is where the trees are older than the arrangement between them and us, supplicant. It is where the hist that stopped is still standing. An older tree is not a kinder one. It is only a tree that has had longer to decide what it thinks of a person walking under it. Ask about the stilled man if you want the shape of what is owed there, on terms no living person agreed to.

It starts about a day past the last stilt and there is no line drawn on the ground where it starts. People walk in and most of them walk out. The ones who don't come out are not the ones I think about. I think about the stilled man, and I think about who ends up in the rot house afterwards.

You can hear the water change, dry-one. That's the whole of it. The marsh lights are the part everyone asks about and they are the least of it. The water sounds like water for two days and then one morning it sounds like something taking a drink, and if you've any sense that's the morning you turn round.
Good place to not be found. Bad place to be found in. I've done both.
Three go out of here. The road to Gideon is metalled and taxed. The road to Helstrom is neither. The road to Lilmoth is a river with a reputation. Which of the three are you taking?

The road to Archon is four days if the vats haven't flooded and nine if they have. The road to Soulrest I won't send a cart down at all any more, and that's the second season running. And the road to Blackrose, well, you're standing on it.

The road to Thorn, two days, and the last of it is plank. The road to Stormhold, five, and you'll want the boots off at the end of it. I've had both sorts through here this month and the Thorn ones complain less.

Thirteen is the Office's number and it is not a good one. The Western Rootlands and the Stone Wastes share a single entry in most accounts — a hundred and forty miles of difference recorded as a comma. The Valus Ridge is entered twice under two spellings, because two surveyors walked it in the same decade and neither read the other.

Topal Bay is warm and shallow and full and it is ours. Then there's the Padomaic past the heads, which is none of those things. My father crossed the line between them once and talked about it for the rest of his life.
We're Thornmarsh, officially. You'll not hear it said. And the Hive is north of us, and you'll not hear that said either, for a different reason. Do you know which reason?
We hold four of the old imperial forts. Two are roofed. The curfew is mine to call and I call it when the tide is wrong, not when the town is loud. Citizen, people get that backwards.

Everything's filed in the Imperial tongue and about a third of the province can read it. That's not policy, it's just what happened, and the part that surprises people is who the third is. It isn't the Dunmer either, whatever they'll tell you at the factor house, and the Dunmer question is a longer one than that.

You want the nine here? They are here the way a road is here — the Empire laid it and now it's just the ground. And there is the bell that rings on its own maybe twice a year, and the priest has stopped explaining it, and honestly I think he's happier for it.

We keep the Tribunal at home and we keep them quietly here, and the chapel affects not to notice. That is the whole of the tribunal question in this province. If you were raised to the shrine return you will find nowhere here to make it, and you will find that stops mattering to you in about a year. Were you raised to make one?

The first tide is the one you work, and after that you are only wet and in the way. And there have been three months now of the empty nets, and no one at the market will say the words out loud, so they say the weather instead and go home.

The marsh lights are out over the flats most nights, dry-one, and everyone's got a cousin who followed one, and the cousin is always another man's cousin. The drums are the part I'd ask about, if I were the asking sort. They aren't every night. A thing that came every night would only be weather.

The fever was one year and everyone remembers the year. What came after was six, and the Office never gave those a name, so I call them the thin years and people know what I mean without me saying how I know.

What is sung to a tree is not a song in the sense a warmblood means, supplicant, and the hist songs are not songs in that sense either. What is done at the egg-tending is not a ceremony in that sense. Both are closer to what is done for a debt carried so long that the carrying has become the whole of the relation. It is tended. It is not worshipped. That difference is not one this province has ever managed to explain to an Office.

Root water is drawn and drunk and it is not a sacrament. The drowned kin are under and are not gone. Hist debt is carried and was never agreed to. What the sap says is said to one person at a time and is not repeated after. Four things, supplicant, and a warmblood scholar has written a book on each without having done any of them.

Nine fires burn in this town and eight of them will feed you: the hearths are open to anyone who sits down at one, and the ninth is a family matter. And half the coin over my counter this month has been the mudcrab money. It spends fine until the season turns. Have you tried to change any?

The ferrymen aren't a guild and they'd like you to think they are. As for the fishing rights — my grandfather's water is now three men's water and none of the three is me. I've been to the Office about it twice. Do you know what a third visit costs?

You pay the lamp tax whether your street has any lamps on it. Wide-Eye Teel keeps the list of who's paid and she keeps it in her head, and she's never once been wrong, and not one of her neighbours has ever seen her write. The warehouse row is where you go when you can't pay it.

The salt market is the whole reason there is a town on this rock. Okan-Shei has held the west end for thirty years and has never once undercut a rival — a stranger way to trade than cheating, and it has worked better for him. Are you buying salt or selling it?
The rose yard is the old execution ground and there are roses on it now, planted deliberate, by the prison. The town has never once agreed whether the roses are an apology.

The Thorn charter says Thorn is a village and a village pays no gate fee. The charter is a hundred and eleven years old and the Office has stopped answering letters about it. If you break something out here it's the bone-setter or it's the road, and the road's two days.

The listening at Soulrest is kept at the hour the tide turns, and that is not the same hour twice in a year. A person who wishes to attend must know the water rather than the calendar. It is not a test. It is only what the practice is, and the town has arranged its evenings round it, the bone setter included, for longer than there has been a town.

Everything goes through the underwriters' gate and the gate is one man with a stamp. He'll refuse you once as a matter of form. It's the second refusal that means anything, and by then you've paid for the first.

Four rooms decide what a thing is worth here: the Office, the factor house, whatever House business is being done that week, and bank law, which is the only one of the four that's written down. Guess which one moves the price.

The Court sits four days and speaks on three of them. What is decided on the fourth is not written down, because on the fourth day nothing is said at all. The fourth silence, it is called. A warmblood hears that and assumes a secret is being kept. What is being kept is a silence, and it is kept from the Court itself.

Ask anyone here what the Court is for and you'll get the same answer in a different order. Ask what we are owed by it and the room goes quiet, and it isn't a sullen quiet, it's people doing arithmetic.

There's a scribe in this town who was struck off the roll and still comes in every morning and still works. The notary won't call it a removal. She won't call it anything else either. The removal that is not one, and nobody will put a plainer name to it.

There is the sound below, which is what the walkers call it, and not one of them will describe it to me, and I've asked four of them, politely, over a year. There's the drowned post down there too, and a walker on it every day. That isn't a rumour, that's a rota.
The wells are what everyone talks about. Not one of them has said a word about what the tide does now, and it has been doing it longer.

A list is kept of the hatching pool a person came out of, of your egg year, of your clutch mark, and of the second name that was taken afterwards. It is kept by the clutch and it is not kept by the Office. The Office has a list of its own and believes it to be the same list. Supplicant, you have four entries in this province and you have read none of them.

We take one name and we take it in writing. The price of a name is not a thing the form has a box for, and I have watched people decide, at my desk, in about four seconds, which of their names they are prepared to give the Empire. The word they use for what I do here is not a polite one and I think it's fair.

Citizenship comes with the oath. Home leave doesn't. Bridge duty is the one the recruits dodge and it is the one that gets you noticed. Ask the quartermaster for boots twice — the first pair's the ones he wanted rid of!

You talk like the towns. Your accent is not an accusation, it is just the first thing this street noticed about you. Some of us kept the old tongue and some of us kept the third person and most of us kept neither, and the ones who kept both are unbearable at dinner. If you want what the towns say about us, ask, and I will give you the polite half. Which did your house keep?

What is owed is learned standing in the shallows before it is ever learned in words. It is learned again at the first molt. It is settled, for those who go, on the long swim. None of the three is taught by being told about it. What the marsh remembers is a person who did all three, and it has no opinion whatever about one who did none. It is the absence of opinion that frightens the towns, supplicant, and not the debt.

It shows and it does not say, and what the sap showed me is not transferable. The hist that stopped showing anything at all is not thereby dead. It is a tree that has decided, and no appeal is written anywhere against a tree's decision. If you want to know what happens to the old ones, it is this: they go quiet first. It has never been established what the quiet is the beginning of.

Every writ is copied twice: once for the Warden-Scribe's file and once for the second ledger, which is ours. The Office has been told about the first. Do you want to know what we keep from the office, or would you rather not be able to say you had been told?

Two boards. One is cohort business and one is what the Tribune wants, and they are not the same board for a reason. The legion quartermaster posts on neither. Citizen, if you are after work, it is the quartermaster you want.

The Tribune drinks here on the eleventh of the month and it has never been put on a board. There is the quiet route out the back for people who'd rather not walk past him. And one of the faces in this room tells him who used it. I've decided not to mind, and not to ask who informs.

What the house pays us is wine and standing and coin, in that order, and it prefers you not to reckon the third. There are the old cages behind the yard that have not held anything in twenty years and have not been taken down either. Were you asking about the vintage, or were you asking about the cages?

There's a buyer and it isn't the House, not directly, not since the treaty, and who buys is a longer walk than you think. There's the fence at Helstrom who has never once asked me where a thing came from. And there's the count of the taken, kept by a woman in Soulrest, which does not match the Office's count and which she will show to any caller. Does that sound like a trade to you?
The bank toll, the boat tax, the crossing fee, and the surcharge that exists to round the other three up to something a clerk can add in his head. Only the last one is honest about what it is for.

You'll pass a village on that road with the doors all shut properly from the outside and not a soul behind them, and it's the doors that stay with you. If you want to know why the village is empty, the village tally is cut in the post at the turning. The village didn't die. It is the village that moved, and it moved without telling the Office, and the Office still sends a man to count it.

Half of what I treat in outlanders isn't magic and isn't even the marsh. It is the fever they brought with them, the smell they can't stop noticing, breathing here, and what to drink. Fix the last one and three of the others go away on their own. And not one of them believes me about the water!

Warmblood isn't an insult, it's just a fact about you, and you'll stop hearing it as one by the time the mud season has come round twice. Your people here mostly last one. The lodging price is what it is because of how many didn't.

You've been told what the band eats and you've been told what the band owes, and you've been told both by people who have never been south of the ford. Ask me about the naga and you will get it from someone who was. The road south is open. It has been open the whole time, and the bands stay north of it. Why do you suppose that is?

A well that has gone quiet is not empty, supplicant, and it is not a thing that is entered. The cistern under the old warehouse has been quiet two years and has been entered twice, and there are people on that street who will tell you about the thing in the cistern. The warehouse key is in two hands now and neither will discuss it. Our losses are being counted somewhere. They are not being counted here.

You want what Tear thinks? Tear thinks it ended. That is the whole of Tear's position and they have held it for two hundred years. Out here the marsh burial from it is still being made, and slavery is still being practised on the water, and if you say either of those in a Dres hall you'll be told you have misunderstood the treaty.

The net price has gone up a third and the fish haven't. Counting by tides is how a man's age is reckoned out here, which sounds pretty until you have had to do it for a child. There's the quiet grave on the point with no name on it and everyone knows the name.

This one cuts. This one does not ask the hist first, friend, and this one knows what that is worth. Egg-tending season the yards go quiet and every hand has gone home. And what the cohort sells is that same sap, on again, which they will deny. Have you seen their manifest?

A man came through here selling the second name off a dead cousin, papers and all. There are the old cages in this trade that have not been opened in years and every runner knows where they stand. There's still a buyer. Not asking who buys.

The fee's set by the Office and the lodging price is set by whoever has a roof, and only one of those has ever been appealed successfully. Add the bank toll and the surcharge and you'll find the roof is cheaper than the paper.
